summary:
Puerto Rico is a territory of the United States, and the full United States federal framework applies on the island: federal statutes, executive orders and agency procedure govern entry, documents, screening, federally funded care and federal custody. The territory's own legislation does not soften that framework; in the area of trans medical care it adds a further restriction of its own.

United States travel documents record sex assigned at birth, and the January 2025 executive order eliminated the X marker, so a trans visitor arriving on United States documents presents a marker that may not match their appearance at inspection.

Airport screening in Puerto Rico follows federal Transportation Security Administration procedure. All luggage is screened and may be subject to a hand search. Prosthetics, including breast forms, are treated as medically necessary equipment and are not counted under the three-liquid rule; medical devices and prosthetics are permitted through the security checkpoint after screening. The National Center for Transgender Equality publishes packing guidance intended to reduce the intrusiveness of such searches, which applies equally at Puerto Rico's airports.

In July 2025 Puerto Rico banned gender-affirming care for anyone under 21 and barred public funding for it. Doctors who violate the ban face up to 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine and permanent loss of their licences. A report by Erin in the Morning described the measure as the most extreme restriction on trans medical care in any United States jurisdiction, pushed through non-public hearings and written with deliberate vagueness that puts affirming parents and physicians at risk of prosecution for facilitating hormone therapy or chest surgery. The same law mandates campaigns by the education and health departments on the risks of trans-affirming care. Health Secretary Carlos Ramos Otero proposed amendments that would have permitted puberty blockers and allowed existing hormone therapy to continue; the enacted text does not adopt them. The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation has announced plans to challenge the ban in court.

No ban on conversion therapy is in force for minors in Puerto Rico. A bill to prohibit it, SB1000, passed the Senate in 2019 with the governor's support but the statehood party caucus in the House blocked a floor vote in March 2019. A later pairing that combined a conversion-therapy ban containing a pastoral exemption for clergy with a religious-freedom measure was announced by Governor Alejandro García Padilla in April 2019 and withdrawn by him on 13 June 2019 after sustained opposition from LGBT advocates, who argued the religious-freedom carve-out would have licensed refusal of service on gender-identity grounds. A comparable religious-freedom bill passed by the legislature in 2017 had been vetoed by Governor Ricardo Rosselló in February 2018.

Federal custody rules govern anyone held in federal facilities in Puerto Rico. The January 2025 executive order directs federal agencies, including the Bureau of Prisons, to recognise only two sexes, and federal practice has since placed transgender inmates in facilities congruent with their sex assigned at birth rather than their asserted gender identity. The American Civil Liberties Union reported that transgender women had been transferred to men's prisons, told they would be, or moved to solitary confinement, and the Bureau of Prisons stopped reporting how many transgender people it holds. Advocates state that the order conflicts with the Prison Rape Elimination Act, which requires that housing decisions for transgender inmates rest on an individual safety assessment. No separate Puerto Rico Department of Corrections policy on trans-inmate housing, special unit or ruling was located.

Puerto Rico's hate crime statutes were amended in 2002 to include sexual orientation and gender identity as protected characteristics, and the territory is also covered by the United States federal Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. 2020 was the first year anyone in Puerto Rico was charged with a hate crime: Sean Díaz de León and Juan Pagán Bonilla were charged after Bonilla confessed that he and Díaz de León murdered two transgender women on 22 April 2020. In January 2021 Governor Pedro Pierluisi declared a state of emergency over continuing murders, assaults and rape of transgender people on the island.

Territory-level anti-discrimination protection is narrower than the hate crime statutes suggest. An omnibus bill, House Bill 1725, passed the House 43-6 in November 2009 and would have barred discrimination on sexual orientation grounds in employment, public transport and public facilities, business transactions and housing, but the Senate held no hearings after Senate President Thomas Rivera Schatz said it would not be approved. The measure that did pass, Senate Bill 238, signed 29 May 2013, was amended in the House so that it applies only to employment discrimination; public facilities, housing and business transactions remain uncovered by territory law. In 2013 the legislature also passed House Bill 488, signed 29 May 2013, extending domestic violence protections to all households regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
The 2025 care ban is described in the reporting as the most sweeping such restriction enacted anywhere in the United States, which places Puerto Rico outside the range of comparable state-level rules rather than at the moderate end of them.

Same-sex marriage in Puerto Rico was established through federal litigation rather than local legislation: four same-sex couples joined the federal marriage suit filed in March 2014, the Ada Conde Vidal case, with Lambda Legal and Puerto Rico Para Todas intervening. Partner recognition for visitors therefore rests on a federal court outcome, not on territory statute.

The record on religious-freedom measures is one of sustained defeat for their sponsors: a 2017 bill was vetoed in February 2018, and the 2019 pairing was withdrawn in June 2019 after opposition from LGBT advocates and a public dissent by Senator Zoe Laboy, a co-sponsor of the conversion-therapy measure. Advocates also defeated the SB1253/SB1254 combination outright.

Protection against violence rests on two overlapping layers, the territory's 2002 hate crime amendment and the federal hate crimes statute, while the machinery of response includes a gubernatorial state of emergency dating from January 2021. Whether that declaration carries funded enforcement capacity is not established by the sources.
localsOnly:
Residents are covered against discrimination in employment by the 2013 law signed on 29 May 2013, after the House narrowed the bill. Employment is the only area the territory statute reaches; housing, public facilities and business transactions are left to federal law and to no territory-level prohibition at all.

Household-level domestic violence protections have applied regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity since House Bill 488 was signed on 29 May 2013.

Residents who are 18, 19 or 20 fall within the July 2025 care ban, and the ban's vagueness is described as exposing parents who facilitate hormone therapy or chest surgery to prosecution alongside their physicians. Existing patients whose treatment was already underway are not protected in the enacted text; the health secretary's proposed amendment to allow continuation of hormone therapy was not adopted.

The education and health departments are required by the 2025 law to run public campaigns on the risks of trans-affirming care, so residents can expect institutional messaging through schools and health services.

Minors remain exposed to conversion therapy in the absence of a prohibition; the 2019 ban bill died in the House despite Senate passage and governor support.

The Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation has stated an intention to litigate the care ban, and territory-wide response to violence against transgender people has included a state of emergency declared in January 2021.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Puerto Rico LGBTQ+ Federation's announced legal challenge to the July 2025 care ban has been filed, and its outcome, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

No territory Department of Corrections policy, special unit or judicial ruling on trans-inmate housing was located. In the absence of such a policy, federal Bureau of Prisons practice governs, but how that practice is applied inside Puerto Rico facilities specifically is not documented in the sources.

Whether any doctor or parent has in fact been charged under the 2025 care ban is not established by the sources; the vagueness of the statute is reported as the exposure, not as a documented prosecution.

Conversion therapy for minors is unregulated in territory law following the failure of the 2019 bills. Actual prevalence of the practice, and whether professional licensing bodies act against it, are not sourced here.

The January 2021 state of emergency is documented as a declaration; its funding, duration and implementing measures are not resolved by these sources. Reporting on the 2020 hate crime charges records the charges and a confession but not the trial outcome.
